final_answer:
Ice floats on water due to the unique molecular structure of water and the behavior of hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, molecules are in constant motion, forming and breaking hydrogen bonds rapidly. When water freezes, the molecules arrange into a hexagonal crystalline lattice stabilized by hydrogen bonds. This structure creates a more open, less dense arrangement compared to liquid water. 

In liquid water, molecules pack more closely together, whereas in ice, the hydrogen bonds fix the molecules in a rigid, spaced-out pattern. This lower density of ice (about 90% of liquid water’s density) allows it to float. This property is crucial for ecosystems, as floating ice insulates bodies of water, preventing them from freezing entirely and preserving aquatic life.
